content.summary_of_the_paper: This manuscript addresses posterior sampling in computational imaging by normalizing flows. The method leverages a probabilistic interpretation of a classical regularized energy and requires no training data. The authors propose several strategies to improve performance, including a gradient boosting scheme and a stratified sampling method for variance reduction. Experimental results show some improvement over several baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The manuscript addresses an important topic---uncertainty quantification in imaging problems. The problem definition and setting is clearly stated and the ideas of gradient boosting and alternative sampling strategies indeed seem to improve performance.

On the critical side, my main objections are a lack of novelty and the clarity of exposition. The manuscript is very similar to the work of Sun and Bouman. The derivation on page 4 is really an idea from their paper but this is not explicitly stated. Also, since an introductory discussion is missing, I suspect that readers not familiar with Sun and Bouman's AAAI paper could find it hard to follow. The novelty in the present contribution consists of modifications in the architecture and in the training / sampling strategy, but these are (in my opinion) comparatively minor contributions.

After reading the first 4 pages of the paper it is still not clear what the authors do; up to this point everything is a description of earlier work. Page 5 describes Lipschitz regularization by random sampling and gradient boosted normalizing flows. Both techniques have been described in prior work. The authors cite Gianquinto & Banerjee when talking about the overfitting risk but later on they don't state that gradient boosting normalizing flows is an idea of Gianquinto & Banerjee, and they present it as if it is their own contribution.

A number of motivating statements are made without supporting evidence (either numerical or references). In the introduction the authors write "However, increasing model depth will result in overfitting, as well as making sampling and computing inefficient. The essential assumption of invertibility is also potentially violated along with instability issues caused by the aggregation of numerical errors. The imprecision and variation in flow-based models induce additional uncertainties." Some of these statements intuitively ring true but flows are still very successfully applied and inverted in numerous applications. Do you observe these severe issues in your experiments? Can you provide supporting ablations? Or is there a reference that does so?

There are many statements that I find hard to understand. In the introduction you write "Moreover, the variation in posterior distribution caused by latent space sampling is also non-negligible for the evaluation of the total reconstruction uncertainty." difficult to understand. Which sampling are you referring to here? (I'll come back to this question below.)

In many places you talk about the "flexibility" of your models or the posterior, as something separate for expressivity, but I do not understand what you mean by that. (For example the last paragraph in 4.1 says "... we develop ... RGF ... with enhanced stability, expressivity, and flexibility.")


In 4.1 the authors suggest that the deep image prior is an example of a prior distribution p(x) but this is not true; DIP is an image reconstruction method / framework which leverages the inductive bias of convolutional neural networks and does not define any explicit probabilistic prior, at least not in an obvious way.


The authors repeat this statement often: "The numerical errors introduced in both forward and inverse mapping will aggravate the imprecision and instability which renders the architecture non-invertible and results in uncontrollable model uncertainties that are intractable to characterize." But again, we know that flows are used very successfully in numerous applications. Sun and Bouman in particular use these same ideas to samples posterior in the radiointerferometric inverse problem (black hole imaging). In this sense, I find such statements somewhat exaggerated.

Section 4.2.2. again opens with "However, a deeper structure of flows often renders instability and uncertainty caused by aggregation of the numerical errors." -> (please mend the broken sentence) I feel that the authors are trying very hard to make this point but without providing convincing evidence for some dramatic breakdown.

The first sentence in 4.3 is "Rather than using simple random sampling (SRS) with a larger variance, Latin Hypercube Sampling (LHS) is an ideal candidate with variance reduction, which is generalized in terms of a spectrum of stratified sampling, referred to as partially stratified sampling (PSS), which shows to reduce variance associated with variable interaction but LHS reduces variance associated with additive (main) effects." 

As much as I tried I do not understand what the authors mean.

My understanding fails at two levels: the clarity of prose and the problem statement that the authors are addressing. Since flows push forward distributions to distributions, it is not 100% clear what should be fixed at this point. Are you effectively changing the distribution in the latent space? Are the samples generated by your strategy independent? If not, then why is it true that you are still fitting the true posterior? (I assume this can be shown but I could not find an explanation in your manuscript.)

Soon after the authors write: "To better explore all possible inverse solutions, we propose to leverage a maximin criteria - maximizes the minimum distance between all pairs of points, Xn = argmaxmin{d(xi,xk) : i ̸= k = 1,...,M} where d(x,x′) = 􏰎Mk=1(xi − x′k)2 is the Euclidean distance. Instead of random pair, these criteria will greatly improve the space-filling properties of LPSS, specifically in high-dimensional space." Here I again cannot understand the sentence.

The paragraph ends with "Note that, unlike quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) methods (Caflisch et al., 1998), e.g., Sobol sequence shown in Fig. 6 as well, which are limited in high dimensional problem (Kucherenko et al., 2015), but LPSS (not a QMC) works well with space-filling property and variance reduction in high dimensions."

Once again, I find the writing very unclear and difficult to parse.

Another sentence from the same paragraph is "Instead of random pair, these criteria will greatly improve the space-filling properties of LPSS, specifically in high-dimensional space."---but how do you support this claim, especially in high dimension? There is no theory, numerics, nor pointers to the literature.

The first paragraph in 4.4 ends with "Note that all the flow-based models tend to have a better representational capability as the depth increases but we fix their depth in four blocks to perform a fair comparison." which seems partially at odds with the claims earlier in the manuscript that depth is detrimental. If we can obtain better performance on this task simply by increasing depth, then why not do it?

There is something strange going on with the MRI reconstructions. Why do all reconstructed images in Figure 3 have some periodic blocking artifacts? These reconstructions do not look very good (although it is hard to say more from the small figures). 

I have a hard time understanding the comparisons and the claims about variance reduction. The variance of what is being reduced? I assume of the learned posterior. But if you are training the model with an alternative sampling strategy, are you also sampling with that strategy at inference time? And are the likelihoods that you compute with this sampling strategy the true likelihoods defined by the model or not?

Finally, I could not find any ablations that quantify the influence of Lipschitz regularization.



### Prose and small things

I started making a list but there were quite a few issues so I would just like to suggest that the authors put in a deliberate effort into 

- What does it mean that "the statistics of latent distribution are conservatively propagated"
- "Unfortunately, the inverse process x = F^-1(y) proceeds in the opposite direction, which is a nontrivial task since it is often ill posed." -> please remove "Unfortunately"
- "make accurate uncertainty estimation to be a nontrivial task" -> please remove "to be"

- p3: the sentence "density improves ..." should begin with a capital letter
- p4: where \pi() is a constant -> I assume a constant with respect to \phi

- p5: "Typically, the coupling blocks show an exploding inverse effect because the singular values of the forward mapping tend to zero as depth increases" -> I assume you mean the singular values of the Jacobian?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Clarity should be greatly improved; novelty is in my opinion modest (see above and below); the work seems to be reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: While this paper addresses an important problem, I cannot recommend acceptance in its current form. The main reason is limited novelty: the idea of using flows to learn a posterior for a single image (according to a MAP interpretation of a regularized loss) has been proposed by Sun and Bouman. That constitues the bulk of the present method. The way the manuscript is written does not make it clear that the ideas comes from prior works. The authors make some modifications to the architecture used by Sun and Bouman but those are comparatively minor. Again, gradient boosting normalizing flows have been proposed by Gianquinto & Banerjee but this is also never stated (Gianquinto & Banerjee are cited in a different context). The idea to employ stratified sampling is interesting but I would like to see more justification in the context of posterior fitting (per comments above). The writing needs a lot of work---there are many parts of the manuscript that I could simply not understand. Finally, there are problems with the experiments: the MRI reconstructions contain strange artifact which should not be there, and it would be nice to see ablations that examine the influence of the different components of the framework.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers image reconstruction problems without ground-truth or training data. The authors consider utilizing an invertible generative model given by a normalizing flow to parameterize the image posterior from noisy measurements. Learning the image posterior also aids in providing estimates of reconstruction uncertainty and potentially allows one to capture multi-modality of the space of possible reconstructions. While previous work has shown this approach can be successful, one issue with normalizing flows is that inversion can be numerically unstable and have limited expressibility due to common architectural choices in the model. Thus, the main contribution of the proposed work is to increase stability of this approach and improve expressability of the model by utilizing 1) bi-Lipschitz regularization, 2) gradient boosting, and 3) variance-reduced latent sampling. The authors validate their approach on several datasets, including problems inspired by MRI and black hole imaging, and showcase improvements to previous approaches.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:**
- The method investigates a challenging problem, which is to solve inverse problems without access to ground-truth data or training images.
- The additional components integrated into the framework are well-motivated, e.g., increasing expressability and stability of normalizing flows for posterior sampling.
- The approach improves upon previous methods in several interesting tasks. 

**Weaknesses:**
- The novelty of the work on a conceptual-level is marginal, as it mainly improves upon an existing method with certain architectural/training improvements.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity:** The paper is well-written and highlights the main ideas of the work well. 

**Novelty and significance:** Conceptually, the work is heavily inspired by Sun & Bouman, which was the first to use a normalizing flow to sample from the posterior without training data. The core contributions of this work lie in improving upon this method in the training and architectural improvements to the flow model. These modifications showcase improvements, so the significance is non-trivial.

**General comments:**
- I would recommend changing the ‘on’ in the title to ‘for’
- The authors note that the computational cost of the method is quite high, especially since the normalizing flow model is trained on image space. I was curious as to how long the method took to train as well, especially given the additional components of the bi-lipschitz regularization, gradient boosting, etc.?
content.summary_of_the_review: While the fundamental idea of the proposed method is inspired by previous work, there seem to be significant improvements made to the approach through the use of stability-inducing regularization techniques and architectural improvements. I think the work is a fairly solid contribution.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a way to regularise and train normalizing flows for uncertainty estimation in imaging inverse problems. Crucially for every measurement they have a different flow model trained like Deep Probabilistic Imaging, Sun and Bouman, AISTATS 2020 and Trumpets, Kothari et al UAI 2021.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- The authors attempt to bring a lot of previously proposed ideas: that of spectral regularization, gradient boosting, LHS/LPSS to uncertainty estimation. 

Weaknesses:
- The paper could help a lot from a rewrite. In a lot of areas the authors could make the writing much tighter and crisper (ex. abstract, the entire section 3 could be made one para and included in related work, the experiments: explain why did you choose to make images so small (160 → 32), why choose a small RGF model (24 transformations only)? )
- Computing uncertainty estimation for a single set of measurements may not be very indicative of model performance as a general framework. I would recommend trying for multiple measurements and see if the model performs well across all of them. For D.1 and D.2 show 5 samples but do not show if the UQ is correct. If the paper is about uncertainty estimation shouldn’t the uncertainty be higher in the missing portions of the image.
- It would be great if the authors could discuss the effects of gradient boosting and spectral regularization separately via ablative studies.
- I am not quite sure but if the problem is truly ill-posed, wouldn’t you want a variety of possible solutions (like the black hole example). In light of this, why is a lower standard deviation better? In the black hole case you know there are two modes but what if we have no such a priori information. If we grade posterior models based on their std deviation a model that captures a single mode and samples only close to that is better even though it may miss all the other modes. Can the authors elaborate on this?
- There are a lot of papers now around UQ and injective flows (Trumpets, Kothari et al, UAI 2021,  M-flows, Brehmer and Cranmer, NeurIPS, 2020) that might be good to compare against.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The writing is hard to follow at times because it is quite fluffy. I encourage the authors to considerably strengthen the paper by trying to think of the main paper as the only space they have. Often they reference imp equations in the Appendix and that considerably breaks flow. At times the writing just is not clear:
    - Pg 2. The imprecision and variation in flow-based models: what does variation here refer to?
    - Pg 2. Statistics to the latent space are conservatively propagated: what exactly does this mean?
    - Pg 4. para before 4.2: “Noted that the flow-based model is very critical and sensitive to uncertainty estimation and quantification within 
      this variational framework.” What does it mean for a model to be “critical” and “sensitive” to UQ?

- The paper is limited in novelty but brings an interesting mix of ideas to uncertainty estimation. Unfortunately their writing makes it seem that they are claiming novelty to these ideas when they just bring it to posterior estimation and UQ. It would help the readers if the authors state this explicitly.
- [Reproducibility] The authors share some code snippets and will hopefully submit the code upon decision. To the author’s advantage, since these models are very small they are easy to try and reproduce with a single GPU.
content.summary_of_the_review: I recommend the authors redo the writing on this paper with a hard 9 page limit in mind (without appendices), make conservative claims and check if the results perfectly reflect the claims made. As of its current state, unfortunately I cannot recommend acceptance.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a framework for solving inverse problems without training data by learning the posterior distribution of target images, parameterized as normalizing flows. Furthermore, authors introduce three improvements to their reconstruction method: 1) a bi-directional regularizer on an approximation of the Lipschitz-constant of the flow model and its inverse, aimed at reducing instabilities due to numerical errors;  2)  a gradient boosting method for flow models that progressively adds new components to the network, increasing expressiveness while avoiding producing very deep flow architectures; and 3) a latent sampling method that reduces variance due to variable interactions and additive effects in the posterior samples. Numerical experiments on accelerated MRI reconstruction and interferometric blackhole imaging demonstrate that the proposed method produces high-quality samples more consistently compared with other related works.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strenghts:

-  The paper is overall well-written and fairly easy to follow. It is organized in a logical manner.

- The paper's motivation is clear and it is very relevant to the ML community. Designing efficient algorithms  for inverse problems that can produce high quality reconstructions without training data is very important, as in many scientific applications ground truth images are extremely scarce or non-existent.  Furthermore, quantifying the uncertainty in the reconstructions facilitates gaining the trust of practitioners in deep learning methods that typically lack interpretability.

- The proposed method appears to have consistently higher precision (lower pixelwise standard deviation in generated posterior samples)  than other comparable methods.

Weaknesses:

- I have doubts with respect to the scaling of the proposed algorithm to higher dimensional problems. The experiments were performed on low-resolution images (up to 128x128, but typically lower), and therefore it is difficult to determine how applicable the proposed method is in practice. For instance, in medical image reconstruction 320x320 is a typical resolution. 

- Experimental details on the run-time of training and sampling from the models is missing. This information would be crucial in comparing the various methods. All the added techniques (bi-directional regularization, gradient boosting, specific sampling method) seem to considerably increase the computational cost and a more in-depth discussion on the compute and memory complexity of these techniques would be very helpful.

- The experimental results are reported based on single images, and therefore I am unsure how cherry-picked the results are in the tables.

- The novelty of the paper is somewhat limited. Normalizing flows in a similar framework have been used for inverse problems in [1], bi-directional finite differences regularization in this form has been proposed in [2] and the gradient boosting scheme for normalizing flows has been proposed in [3]. Authors should consider clarifying the original contribution in this work. 

[1] Whang, J., Lindgren, E. and Dimakis, A., 2021, July. Composing normalizing flows for inverse problems. In *International Conference on Machine Learning* (pp. 11158-11169). PMLR.

[2] Behrmann, J., Vicol, P., Wang, K.C., 
Grosse, R. and Jacobsen, J.H., 2021, March. Understanding and mitigating
 exploding inverses in invertible neural networks. In *International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics* (pp. 1792-1800). PMLR.

[3]  Giaquinto, R. and Banerjee, A., 2020. Gradient boosted normalizing flows. *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems*, *33*, pp.22104-22117.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: the paper is clear in most parts.
Quality: the paper demonstrates promising results, however due to the small datasets (single image in most cases) the method has been evaluated on, and the lack of comparison with respect to run-time, memory and compute, it is difficult to fully evaluate the merit of the work.
Novelty: To my understanding, the original contribution of this paper is combining several existing methods (NF for parameterizing posterior, bi-directional regularization, gradient boosting for NF, Latinized Partially Stratified Sampling) into a single algorithm.  
Reproducibility: no source code is provided to reproduce the results.

Minor comments:

- I am unsure why lower pixelwise standard deviation on the posterior samples is necessarily better. The estimator might have a specific bias, for instance a characteristic reconstruction artifact, that is present consistently on all samples but in fact reduces sample quality.

- The subsection on gradient boosting is difficult to follow. Why is a term missing from the variational lower bound in equation 9?

- Possible typo in Eq (5) in the regularizer term.

- Equations from the appendix have been referenced multiple times in the main paper. Either the relevant equations and corresponding discussion should be moved from the appendix to the main paper, or the equation references should be removed from the main paper. 

- Typo on the last line of page 5.

- Typo in 5.1 "Regrading"

- I am not sure what the first sentence on page 6 means, possible typo/missing word.

content.title: Robust Generative Flows on Reliable Image Reconstruction without Training Data
content.abstract: A key application of computational imaging is to determine the hidden information from a set of observed but sparse measurements. To fully characterize the uncertainty naturally induced by the sparse measurements, a robust inverse solver that is able to estimate the complete posterior of the unrecoverable targets is therefore important, with a potential to probabilistically interpret the observational data for decision making. In this work, we propose a deep variational framework that leverages a deep generative model to learn an approximate posterior distribution for quantifying image reconstruction uncertainty without training data. This is achieved by parameterizing the target posterior using a flow-based model and minimizing their KL divergence. To perform accurate uncertainty estimation, we propose a robust flow-based model where the stability is enhanced by adding bi-directional regularization and the expressivity is improved by using gradient boosting. We also found that the statistics of latent distribution are conservatively propagated to the posterior distribution through an invertible transformation and therefore introduce a space-filling design to achieve significant variance reduction on both latent prior space and target posterior space.  We demonstrate our method on several benchmark tasks and two real-world applications (fastMRI and black hole image reconstruction) and show that it achieves a reliable and high-quality image reconstruction with robust uncertainty estimation.
